nameStory: The name 'crowberry' comes from the small, dark berries that crows and other birds love to eat. The scientific name Empetrum literally means 'upon a rock' in Greek, perfectly describing where you'll find this tough little plant growing in rocky, windswept places. Indigenous peoples across the Arctic have many names for this important food source, including 'paurngaq' in Inuktut and 'asiavik' in Iñupiaq.
description: Black crowberry is a low-growing, evergreen shrub that hugs the ground like a living carpet in harsh, exposed places. It rarely grows taller than 6 inches, spreading outward instead to form dense mats that can cover large areas. The plant looks almost moss-like from a distance, with tiny needle-shaped leaves and small dark berries that appear in late summer. This incredibly tough little survivor thrives where few other plants can, making it a true champion of New England's most challenging environments.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, needle-like evergreen leaves that are dark green and feel leathery to the touch. They're arranged densely along the stems and curve slightly backward, giving branches a bottlebrush appearance when viewed closely.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, low mats that sprawl across the ground, rarely rising above 6 inches tall. The woody stems branch frequently and root where they touch the ground, creating an interconnected carpet.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round berries that ripen from red to deep purple-black in late summer. They're about the size of a peppercorn, feel slightly dry rather than juicy, and have a mildly sweet, somewhat bland taste.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous pink or purplish flowers that appear in spring, tucked close to the stems. Each flower is only about 2-3mm across and easily overlooked among the dense foliage.

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Almost always found growing in extremely harsh conditions - exposed rocky summits, coastal bluffs, or boggy areas where most other plants struggle to survive.

habitat: Look for black crowberry in New England's most extreme environments - the windswept summits of mountains above treeline, rocky coastal headlands battered by salt spray, and acidic bogs. It thrives in poor, acidic soils where few competitors can survive, often growing alongside other hardy plants like mountain cranberry and Labrador tea. You'll find the largest populations on the highest peaks of the White Mountains and along Maine's rocky coastline.

seasonality.spring: Tiny pinkish flowers appear in May and June, though they're so small you'll need to look closely to spot them among the dense evergreen foliage.
seasonality.summer: The plant maintains its dark green carpet appearance while berries begin developing from the spring flowers, starting out red before ripening.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to their characteristic deep purple-black color by late August and September, providing an important food source for migrating birds.
seasonality.winter: Remains green and identifiable under snow, with the low-growing mats often completely buried but still alive beneath the white blanket.

funFact: Black crowberry can live for over 100 years, with some individual plants in the Arctic estimated to be several centuries old - making that humble little mat on a mountaintop potentially older than the oldest trees in many New England forests!
confusionNotes: At first glance, it might be confused with mountain cranberry, but crowberry's leaves are much more needle-like and its berries are darker and less juicy. Remember: crowberry needles, cranberry ovals - and cranberry has much more obvious red berries that are noticeably tart and juicy when bitten.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'blackberry' in some regions like western Alaska, this plant is completely unrelated to the thorny blackberry bushes that produce the large, clustered berries we know from grocery stores. The name similarity is purely coincidental based on berry color.
compareHints: Black crowberry is the only Empetrum species commonly found in New England, though purple crowberry (Empetrum atropurpureum) occurs rarely in northern areas. Purple crowberry has slightly more upright growth and purplish-tinged foliage, while black crowberry stays flatter to the ground with purely green leaves. Within the heath family, crowberry's needle-like leaves and extreme mat-forming habit make it quite distinctive from relatives like blueberries and mountain laurel.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple crowberry differs from its close relative black crowberry mainly in berry color - purple crowberry fruits have a distinctly purple-black hue while black crowberry fruits are pure black.
